text.MAP1_RESULT: Dam gauges cluster where the big reservoirs are: California (76), the Pacific Northwest (70), the Mid-Atlantic (52), the South Atlantic-Gulf (46) and the Ohio (41). The Tennessee, Lower Mississippi and Souris-Red-Rainy regions have one each. 404 of the 458 controls come from their dam gauge's own region. New England (7 controls for 28 dam gauges), California (46 for 76) and the Great Basin (15 for 18) ran out, and the other 54 were borrowed nearby: New England's from the Mid-Atlantic, Ohio, Tennessee and Great Lakes regions, California's from the Pacific Northwest, Lower and Upper Colorado and Missouri, the Great Basin's from the Lower Colorado and Pacific Northwest. HUC 01 to 09 hold 217 dam gauges and 217 controls, HUC 10 to 18 hold 241 and 241.
text.MAP1_CONCLUSION: East against West and mostly region by region, the controls sample the same climates as the dam gauges. Borrowing now stays close to home, but California's 30 borrowed controls sit in eight other states, from Washington to New Mexico. Borrowed controls are hollow in Figure 2 and tagged in the table.
text.AREA_RESULT: The match held for small basins and failed for large ones, and the 3x rule made it looser. Below 500 km² the median control is 0.96 times the area of its dam gauge and 84 % of pairs are within a factor of 1.5. Above 5,000 km² the median control is 0.14 times the size and 1 % of pairs are within a factor of 1.5: undammed rivers that large are rare among the training gauges. Overall the controls are smaller (median 641 against 1,400 km²); 36 % of pairs are within a factor of 1.5 and 45 % within a factor of 2, down from 47 % and 57 % on the 1.5x set.
text.AREA_CONCLUSION: Size could confound the comparison, so it was checked. In the 167 pairs matched within a factor of 1.5, the dam gauge leads its control by +0.005 (95 % interval +0.001 to +0.016); in the 291 looser pairs it leads by +0.011 (+0.006 to +0.018). The difference comes from the dam side: dam-gauge gains rise a little with area (Spearman ρ 0.12), while the controls' change does not track area (ρ 0.02). The loose match does not create the dam effect, and the well-matched figure is the conservative one. A rebuilt set should let large dam gauges share controls.
text.F1_RESULT: All dam gauges: median change +0.007 (95 % interval +0.004 to +0.013), 291 up and 167 down (sign test p = 7e-9); 88 gain more than 0.1 and 8 lose more than 0.1. Split by placement: +0.020 (+0.009 to +0.032; 150 of 214 up) where the dam is on the gauge's own reach, +0.004 (+0.0004 to +0.007; 141 of 244 up) where it is further up. By area ratio it looks the same: +0.017 at the 312 gauges within 1.5 times the dam's area, +0.003 at the 145 between 1.5 and 3 times. Controls: median 0.000 (−0.0003 to +0.0005), 233 up and 225 down; 15 gain more than 0.1. A dam gauge beats its own control by a median of +0.009 (+0.005 to +0.012), ahead in 282 of 458 pairs (p = 8e-7). The one-parameter plain bucket gets most of the gain (+0.006 at dam gauges). Per-gauge KGE falls slightly in both groups (−0.002 at dam gauges, −0.003 at controls) because the fit maximises NSE, though the dam-gauge median KGE rises from 0.685 to 0.692.
text.F1_CONCLUSION: The bucket helps below dams and leaves the controls alone: at 267 of 458 controls the tuned response time sits on the 0.05-day grid floor, which is pass-through. The gain is concentrated at dams on the gauge's own reach. Further down, undammed tributaries dilute the release, and the gauges admitted by the 3x rule (1.5 to 3 times the dam's area) gain a median of only +0.003. That is why the per-gauge median fell from +0.017 on the 1.5x set to +0.007 here. The gains land where the no-dam model is worst (median no-dam NSE 0.32 at the 88 gauges that gain more than 0.1, against 0.68 at the rest), so the group median NSE rises from 0.619 to 0.670 while the typical gauge moves by 0.007.
text.MAP2_RESULT: Dam-gauge gains are largest in the Southwest and on the flood-control reservoirs of the plains and Midwest: median change +0.124 in the Rio Grande (10 gauges), +0.078 in Texas-Gulf (6), +0.051 in Arkansas-White-Red (12), +0.048 in the Upper Mississippi (25), and +0.025 in both the Missouri (30) and the Upper Colorado (17). New England, the Great Lakes and the Ohio gain little (+0.001 to +0.007). California (76 dam gauges, −0.001, 31 up and 45 down) and the Great Basin (18, −0.009, 8 up and 10 down) lose slightly, and East and West come out even (median +0.007 each). The control map is mostly hollow circles. 7 of the 15 controls that gain more than 0.1 are lowland swamp and spring-fed rivers of the South Atlantic-Gulf region (Santa Fe, Myakka, Econfina, Pearl), where natural storage that the no-dam model lacks plays the reservoir's part.
text.MAP2_CONCLUSION: The hypothesis holds on the plains and in the Southwest and fails in the far West. 31 of California's 76 dam gauges sit below hydropower dams, and many Sierra projects route water through tunnels and powerhouses around the gauged reach. The Great Basin's losses are on the Truckee, Little Truckee and Weber, below Lake Tahoe, Stampede, Boca and Echo, whose releases follow water rights and irrigation demand. A bucket fed only by natural inflow cannot take water out of the river or release it on that schedule. The learned release may need a diversion or loss term, or those gauges should be scored separately.
text.F2_RESULT: The dam median sits right of the control median in 13 of 18 regions. The exceptions are Tennessee and Lower Mississippi (one dam gauge each), the Great Lakes and the Great Basin (ties, at +0.001 and −0.009), and California (−0.001 against 0.000). Control medians stay within 0.01 of zero everywhere except the two one-gauge regions, Lower Mississippi (+0.06) and Souris-Red-Rainy (+0.03). The largest dam medians are the Lower Colorado (+0.14, 2 gauges), Rio Grande (+0.12), Texas-Gulf (+0.08), Arkansas-White-Red (+0.05) and Upper Mississippi (+0.05).
text.F2_CONCLUSION: The dam effect is broad but uneven. It is strongest where storage is large against flow and the no-dam model is weakest, and absent where operations decouple release from inflow. The Rio Grande's dam gauges have a median regulation of 2.3 and a median no-dam NSE of −0.11; the Ohio's have 0.14 and 0.79.
text.F3_RESULT: The median gain is +0.005 with storage up to a tenth of annual flow (74 gauges), +0.007 from 0.1 to 0.5 (170), +0.011 from 0.5 to 1 (98) and +0.024 from 1 to 2 (63), then 0.000 above 2 (53). Gauges below a chain of large dams gain more (+0.010, 223) than gauges below a single one (+0.006, 235). Controls sit at 0.000. One point is clipped at the top: Rio Hondo below Diamond A Dam, New Mexico, goes from −17.5 to −11.2 on a channel that carries less than 0.01 m³/s on 88 % of days.
text.F3_CONCLUSION: The gain grows with regulation up to one or two years of storage and then collapses. The most heavily regulated gauges (Courtright, Eagle Nest, Stampede, Boca) sit below reservoirs that carry water across years, whose releases follow operating rules, demand and snowpack more than this year's inflow. A linear bucket with a seasonal response time cannot follow that, and at Courtright the fit ran into the 1,000-day wall. The release law needs a cap on T₀ and, for these dams, information beyond inflow.
text.F7_RESULT: Big Muddy River at Plumfield, Illinois, below Rend Lake (flood control, 228 MCM), is one of the gauges the 3x rule added (1.56 times the dam's area). The model's January storm peak of 303 m³/s is cut to 117 against an observed 123, and the recession is held up. That year's NSE rises from −0.07 to 0.90, and over all test years from 0.003 to 0.872, with T₀ 4.8 days. Below Cannonsville Dam on the West Branch Delaware, New York (water supply), observed summer flow averages 15.5 m³/s against the model's 5.5, most likely water stored earlier and released downstream. A bucket can delay water but cannot add it in summer, so the lines barely move (0.540 to 0.546 over the test years). Courtright (hydropower, California): the gauge records a small release that peaks in July. The fit put T₀ on the 1,000-day wall and used the seasonal term to release one smooth pulse in April, which misses (−1.62 to −3.47). Little Fishing Creek, North Carolina, a control: T₀ sits on the 0.05-day floor and the ochre line covers the teal one (test NSE 0.793 with and without it).
text.F7_CONCLUSION: The bucket does what a flood-control reservoir does, and it still works with some tributary inflow between dam and gauge (Big Muddy). It cannot add water in the dry season or release on an operator's calendar (Cannonsville), and where the release has nothing to do with inflow, the fit falls back on the seasonal term alone (Courtright). The release needs a bounded T₀ and some input besides the current inflow, such as storage state.
text.F8_RESULT: The viewer opens on the Kaskaskia River at Shelbyville, Illinois, below Lake Shelbyville (flood control, 256 MCM), in WY2008. The model passes storm peaks of up to 286 m³/s; the gauge records the reservoir's stepped releases, never above 102 m³/s. The tuned bucket (T₀ 29 days, swinging from 6 to 139 days over the year) holds its peak to 93 m³/s and follows the release levels, though not the steps. That year's NSE rises from −0.79 to 0.56, and over 1996-2010 from 0.290 to 0.666.
text.F8_CONCLUSION: A linear store with a seasonal response time gets the volume and timing of a flood-control release roughly right but not the operator's steps. That is the fidelity to expect from the release law as planned. Sort the table by Change to find the gauges where it falls short.
text.CHECK5: A joint run with a learned release on every dam has to lift the dam gauges clearly above the controls: median per-gauge change in test NSE above zero with its 95 % interval clear of zero, dam gain minus control gain positive, and the controls' median test NSE within 0.01 of the no-dam arm's (0.767 here). This offline fit (+0.007 at all dam gauges, +0.020 at on-reach dams, +0.009 over the matched controls, 291 of 458 up) is roughly the ceiling for a per-dam bucket on this inflow; a release predicted from dam attributes should land between zero and it.
text.CAVEATS: Caveats. The fit uses the routed flow at the gauge as the dam's inflow. That is closest to exact for the 214 dams on the gauge's own reach; for the 244 further up, the tributaries between dam and gauge pass through the fitted bucket too, which a dam-level release in ddrs will not do, so check 2 is limited to on-reach dams. Each bucket is chosen on a grid (T₀ from 0.05 to 1,000 days; a and b from −2 to 2): 3 dam gauges hit the 1,000-day wall, and 142 of the 335 dam gauges with an active bucket have a or b on the ±2 edge. The fit maximises NSE, and per-gauge KGE falls slightly at dam gauges and controls. Rio Hondo below Diamond A Dam (no-dam NSE −17.5) would dominate any mean, so every summary here is a median. The drainage-area match is loose above about 1,500 km² (Figure 2).
